9th Bengaluru Space Expo · 7–9 Sept 2026

From a Vizag rooftop to the BSX podium.

The Bengaluru Space Expo at BIEC is one of India's largest space gatherings, organised by CII with ISRO, NSIL and IN-SPACe as partners. The 2026 theme was "Harnessing Space for Global Progress: Innovation, Policy, and Growth". Venkat Vardhan took the podium to put a student-scale, software-defined space story in front of the industry.

  • Meeting India's space ecosystem: agencies, startups, policy makers and students
  • Showing that affordable ground stations and CubeSats can come from tier-2 cities
  • Building partnerships for technology transfer, training and joint missions

Looking up, every clear night.

Telescope observation sessions keep the work grounded in the sky it serves.

Standing on giants.

We study the missions of the world's space agencies and bring the same engineering habits to student-scale hardware. These organisations are our inspiration; SKSS is an independent startup and is not affiliated with them.

ISRO
Indian Space Research Organisation

India's space agency. Chandrayaan-3 touched down near the lunar south pole in August 2023, and Aditya-L1 launched to study the Sun that September.

NASA
National Aeronautics and Space Administration

Apollo to Artemis. Its open CubeSat and small-satellite programmes helped make student missions possible.

NSIL · IN-SPACe
India's space industry ecosystem

NSIL commercialises ISRO technology; IN-SPACe opens Indian space activity to private companies and startups.

ESA · JAXA
Europe and Japan

Their university CubeSat programmes show how classrooms can fly real hardware.

Chandrayaan-3, 30 August 2023

The Pragyan rover imaged the Vikram lander at 69.373° S, 32.319° E. Moments like this are why we build: ground stations that listen, and small satellites that carry the idea further. Image credit: ISRO.

Upcoming missions.

Five CubeSat missions where AI turns a small satellite into a smart observer. They are at the concept and design stage; specifications, sensors and schedules will be finalised through design reviews and testing. Each mission can be built as a student project, a research payload or a commercial demonstrator.

M-01 · Concept stage

Micro-Debris Detection & Population Mapping

Problem: Objects below ~10 cm are very hard to track individually with conventional space-surveillance systems, yet they can still damage spacecraft.

CubeSat solution: A CubeSat payload that detects tiny debris using optical (and, later, radar-assisted) observations plus onboard AI, then estimates debris size, relative direction, relative velocity, possible orbital region and a debris-density map.

Unique part: It does not try to follow only large catalogued objects. It focuses on the small, difficult-to-track population.
Full mission detail

How it works

  • Wide-field optical camera looking at dark sky and star background
  • Frame differencing removes stars; moving points and streaks remain
  • Onboard AI filters real events from noise, hot pixels and cosmic-ray hits
  • Brightness and apparent motion give size and relative-velocity estimates
  • Detections are binned by region and time to build a density map
  • Only compact detection records are sent down, saving bandwidth

Payload and hardware

  • Camera or sensor with a baffle against sunlight
  • Optional radar-assisted ranging as a later research stage
  • ESP32-S3-class or stronger edge processor
  • Timestamp and attitude from the IMU

Outputs

  • Detection list with confidence score
  • Estimated size class and relative velocity
  • Direction vectors and likely orbital region
  • Debris-density map over many passes

Hard parts we will work on

  • Very faint targets and short exposure times
  • Distinguishing debris from stray light
  • Limited power and downlink on a small satellite
  • Calibrating size from brightness without known range

M-02 · Concept stage

Autonomous Space-Weather Shield

Problem: Solar flares and energetic-particle events can disturb spacecraft electronics and communications.

CubeSat solution: Radiation and environmental sensors plus AI detect abnormal conditions, then the satellite automatically enters safe mode, reduces non-essential payload activity, prioritises critical telemetry, records the event and alerts the ground station.

Unique part: The spacecraft makes a local risk decision onboard instead of waiting for a ground command.
Full mission detail

How it works

  • Radiation, magnetometer, temperature and voltage sensors run continuously
  • A baseline of normal conditions is learned and stored
  • AI and threshold logic flag abnormal particle or field conditions
  • A graded response: warn, reduce payload load, safe mode
  • Critical telemetry is prioritised and the event is logged with time stamps
  • An alert beacon goes to the ground station on the next pass

Payload and hardware

  • Radiation or particle-count sensor
  • Magnetometer and temperature sensors
  • Voltage/current monitors on the power board
  • Event log in non-volatile memory

Outputs

  • Space-weather alert with severity
  • Time-stamped event record
  • Payload on/off timeline
  • Dataset to compare with public solar-activity data

Hard parts we will work on

  • False alarms versus missed events
  • Sensor selection within CubeSat power limits
  • Safe-mode recovery logic
  • Testing without a real solar storm (use simulation)

M-03 · Concept stage

AI-Based Early Detection of Atmospheric Re-entry

Problem: Small spacecraft and debris lose altitude and eventually re-enter, but the last stages are hard to predict because atmospheric density keeps changing.

CubeSat solution: Combine atmospheric measurements, orbital parameters, solar activity and historical orbital-decay data in an onboard/ground AI model to estimate abnormal orbital decay and re-entry probability.

Unique part: The CubeSat acts as an in-space atmospheric and orbital data collector, improving re-entry prediction.
Full mission detail

How it works

  • Collect accelerometer, attitude and environment data in low orbit
  • Pull orbital elements and altitude history over time
  • Add solar and geomagnetic activity indices from public sources
  • Train a model on historical decay data and compare with current decay
  • Flag decay faster than predicted and compute a re-entry window
  • Return a probability and a confidence band

Payload and hardware

  • IMU and drag-related sensing
  • GNSS or ground-derived orbit data
  • Space-weather feeds on the ground side
  • Ground AI model, optional lightweight onboard version

Outputs

  • Decay-rate anomaly score
  • Re-entry probability and time window
  • Atmospheric density estimates along the orbit
  • Open dataset for researchers

Hard parts we will work on

  • Density varies with solar activity
  • Needs accurate orbit determination
  • Limited training data for tiny satellites
  • Validating predictions against real re-entries

M-04 · Concept stage

Autonomous Satellite Anomaly Detection

Problem: A spacecraft can develop subtle faults before a major failure, but watching thousands of telemetry parameters from Earth is hard.

CubeSat solution: An onboard AI learns the satellite's normal behaviour and detects anomalies in temperature, battery voltage and current, power generation, attitude, communication, CPU and memory, and payload sensors. It outputs an anomaly score and the probable subsystem.

Unique part: The CubeSat becomes its own AI health-monitoring system. This is closest to our current ESP32-S3 hardware.
Full mission detail

How it works

  • Telemetry from every subsystem is sampled on a fixed schedule
  • The model learns what healthy data looks like across modes
  • New samples are scored against the learned baseline
  • A subsystem attribution step points to the likely cause
  • High scores trigger logging, warnings or safe-mode steps
  • Scores and summaries are sent on the downlink

Payload and hardware

  • All housekeeping sensors on the existing stack
  • TinyML on ESP32-S3 (autoencoder, isolation-style or statistical models)
  • LoRa link for compact anomaly reports
  • Ground tools to retrain and update models

Outputs

  • Anomaly score over time
  • Probable subsystem
  • Health summary packets
  • Training dataset from bench and flight

Hard parts we will work on

  • Learning normal behaviour across orbit day/night
  • Memory and compute limits
  • Avoiding false positives
  • Getting real fault examples (use fault injection on the bench)

M-05 · Concept stage

Intelligent Space-Object Identification

Problem: Optical sensors see many objects against the stars, but telling satellites, rocket bodies, debris and transients apart is difficult.

CubeSat solution: A camera, star-field processing and AI classify observed objects as satellite, rocket body, debris, asteroid/transient or unknown, and compute angular position, brightness, apparent motion, trajectory and a confidence score.

Unique part: It combines star-field navigation, computer vision and space-object classification on a CubeSat.
Full mission detail

How it works

  • Capture image sequences of the sky
  • Match star patterns to find exact pointing (plate solving)
  • Subtract stars and extract moving or transient sources
  • Measure brightness changes, such as tumbling flashes
  • Classify by motion, brightness curve and shape
  • Report class, position, trajectory and confidence

Payload and hardware

  • Star-capable camera with stable optics
  • Plate-solving software on the processor or ground
  • Classifier trained on simulated and real sky data
  • IMU for attitude assistance

Outputs

  • Object class with confidence
  • Angular position and apparent motion
  • Brightness curve
  • Trajectory estimate and unknown-object alerts

Hard parts we will work on

  • Training data for rare classes
  • Pointing stability on a small bus
  • Sunlight and Earthshine contamination
  • Compute budget for onboard vision

Inside the CubeSat.

A CubeSat is a small satellite built from standard 10 cm units (1U is a 10 cm cube). Ours is a stacked-board engineering model that you can open, measure and learn from. Pick a subsystem to explore it.

Drag the 3D model to turn it. Specs below are design targets for our engineering model.

Form factorCubeSat-style stacked-board engineering model
ComputerESP32 / ESP32-S3
RadioLoRa SX1278, SMA antenna port
Energy2600 mAh battery, body-mounted solar panels, power management board
SensorsIMU and environmental module
StructureAluminium frame, removable side panels, threaded inserts
Ground linkRTL-SDR based software ground station in Vizag

The open ground station.

A purely software ground station and open research area in Vizag. Public data access, research projects, CubeSat collaboration. Anyone can participate.

How a signal reaches you.

Our ground station is software-defined: cheap radio hardware does the listening, and software does the rest. Here is the path of a satellite packet.

SatelliteTransmits telemetry from orbit
AntennaHelical or Yagi, on a tripod
RTL-SDRDigitises the radio signal
USB hubSeveral receivers at once
SoftwareTracks, demodulates, decodes
PortalPublic data and research
Track

Predict passes from orbital data and point or schedule the receivers.

Receive

Low-cost SDR dongles tune the satellite's band.

Decode

Demodulate and decode packets in software, with no custom hardware.

Share

Open data access so schools and researchers can use what we collect.

Where we are going.

Our plan, step by step. Each stage builds on the one before it. Dates are targets and will change as we learn.

  1. DoneOpen ground station in Vizag

    Rooftop antennas, SDR receivers and a software workflow that anyone can use for research.

  2. DoneCubeSat engineering model

    A stacked-board model with processing, LoRa radio, power, sensors, frame and removable panels.

  3. NextEnvironmental and flight tests

    Vibration, thermal and battery tests, plus a balloon or high-altitude test of the electronics.

  4. NextRocket avionics and test flights

    Flight computer, telemetry and recovery tested on model rockets before larger vehicles.

  5. VisionVAYU-AI orbital mission

    An AI-enabled CubeSat in orbit, received by our own ground station.

  6. VisionSARVADRISHTI Earth observation

    Satellite imaging and analytics for the planet, from India.

Train like an astronaut.

India is training its own crews for human spaceflight, and the next decade will open the Moon and Mars to a new generation. Our analog astronaut programme brings the mindset, discipline and skills of that world to students and professionals in Visakhapatnam.

From rooftop to red planet.

Eight phases. Real procedures. Real radio contact with our own ground station.

Apply for astronaut training

Phase 1Selection and baseline

Medical screening, fitness tests and a psychological profile so training is safe and fits you.

  • Medical clearance advised
  • Strength, endurance, flexibility tests
  • Motivation and teamwork interview
Phase 2Physical conditioning

Space is physically demanding. Build the base you need for long, intense days.

  • Cardio and strength plan
  • Swimming and water confidence
  • Balance, core and vestibular drills
Phase 3Space academics

The science behind every mission.

  • Orbital mechanics and navigation
  • Spacecraft systems and life support
  • Radiation, microgravity and space medicine
Phase 4Flight and G-force awareness

Understand what launch, re-entry and weightlessness do to the body.

  • Launch and re-entry profiles
  • G-tolerance theory and breathing
  • Motion sickness management
Phase 5Survival and field skills

Be capable when plans change.

  • Land and water survival basics
  • Navigation without GPS
  • First aid and emergency response
Phase 6Mission simulation

Practise as a crew with real procedures.

  • Habitat-style simulations
  • Checklist discipline under time pressure
  • Mission control calls using our ground station
Phase 7Teamwork and psychology

Long missions are won by crews who communicate.

  • Isolation and confined-space exercises
  • Conflict resolution and leadership
  • Stress and sleep management
Phase 8Future missions track

Skills for the next era of exploration.

  • Lunar surface operations and sample collection
  • Mars-analog scenarios and communication delay
  • Robotics, EVA tasks and in-situ resource ideas
Who it is for

Students, young professionals, educators and space enthusiasts.

Formats

Weekend bootcamps, multi-week courses and custom college programmes.

You will leave with

Mission logs, a completed simulation and a certificate of participation from SKSS.

Future missions

Priority roles in our simulation crews for upcoming CubeSat missions.

SKSS analog astronaut training is an educational programme. It is not selection for, or certification by, any space agency.

More training tracks.

Practical training led by the people who build the hardware. Open each track for the full outline. Duration, fees and batch dates are shared on enquiry.

CubeSat Building
Build a working satellite stack from parts to telemetry.
  • CubeSat standards, mission design and subsystems
  • Frame assembly, mounting boards and wiring
  • ESP32 firmware: reading sensors, logging, scheduling
  • LoRa link setup and packet design
  • Battery, solar and power budgeting
  • Bench testing and a final demonstration
Ground Station & SDR
Build a station that receives real signals.
  • Radio basics: frequency, bandwidth, polarisation, link budget
  • RTL-SDR setup and software tools
  • Building and aiming antennas (helical, Yagi, telescopic)
  • Predicting satellite passes and Doppler correction
  • Decoding and storing received data
Model Rocketry
From rocket anatomy to recovery, with safety first.
  • How rockets work: thrust, stability, staging
  • Reading a rocket cutaway: tanks, engine, avionics, recovery
  • Flight computer and altitude telemetry
  • Parachute and recovery design
  • Range safety and launch procedures
AI for Space Data
Use machine learning on telemetry and imagery.
  • Python and data handling for telemetry
  • Anomaly detection on sensor data
  • Image analysis for Earth observation
  • Running tiny models on microcontrollers (ESP32-S3)
Astronomy & Observation
Night-sky sessions with telescopes.
  • Telescope assembly, alignment and tracking
  • Finding planets, the Moon and deep-sky objects
  • Basic astrophotography and observation logs
  • Analog astronaut training concepts
